title: Shakespeare's World
description: Elizabethan London, the Globe, the playing companies

concepts.title: Why Shakespeare
concepts.contentHtml:
William Shakespeare (1564-1616) is, by widespread agreement, the most influential writer in the English language. Roughly 39 plays, 154 sonnets, two long poems. He has been continuously performed for four hundred years.

The cult around him can feel suffocating. Setting it aside: he is also genuinely extraordinary. His language is denser per line than most poets'. His characters surprise themselves. He worked in established forms (history play, tragedy, romantic comedy) and pushed each beyond what had been done before.

The strange fact: he was a working theater professional, not a court poet or a literary intellectual. He wrote scripts to fill seats. The plays' depth came in the doing, not in any grand artistic program.

concepts.title: Elizabethan and Jacobean London
concepts.contentHtml:
Shakespeare's working life ran roughly 1590 to 1613, spanning the late Elizabethan era and the Jacobean period under James I. London was a city of about 200,000 — by far England's largest. The theater was a relatively new mass entertainment.

Public theaters were outside the City of London proper, in Southwark and Shoreditch — outside the jurisdiction of city authorities who disapproved of plays. The Globe, built in 1599 by Shakespeare's company on the south bank of the Thames, held about 3,000 spectators.

Plays competed with other entertainments — bear-baiting, prostitution, brothels. Theater audiences were socially mixed. The cheap 'groundlings' stood in front of the stage; the wealthy sat in galleries. Plays needed to work for both.

This is why Shakespeare's plays mix high poetry with crude jokes, philosophical speeches with sword fights. The form was popular entertainment, and it had to be.

concepts.title: The Playing Companies
concepts.contentHtml:
Shakespeare's career was tied to a single acting company: the Lord Chamberlain's Men, renamed the King's Men after James I's accession in 1603. He was an actor and 'sharer' (part-owner), not just a writer.

This shaped his work. He knew his actors personally. He wrote roles for specific colleagues. Richard Burbage, the lead tragedian, played Hamlet, Lear, Othello, Macbeth — created roles, not adaptations. The company's clown specialist (first Will Kempe, later Robert Armin) shaped the comic roles. The boys playing women's parts had specific vocal ranges and abilities.

Plays were performed in repertory, often a different play each afternoon. Memorization, rehearsal, costume work happened on tight timelines. Plays sometimes had little or no rehearsal beyond an actor's individual study of his lines.

This is the practical machine that produced 'Hamlet' and 'King Lear.' Not a quiet study — a working theatrical company under constant deadline pressure.

concepts.title: Sources
concepts.contentHtml:
Shakespeare almost never invented a plot. He took stories from existing sources and reworked them.

For history plays: Holinshed's Chronicles of England, Scotland, and Ireland.

For Roman plays: North's translation of Plutarch's Lives.

For comedies and romances: Italian novellas, English prose romances, classical sources.

For tragedies: a mix. The plot of Hamlet comes from a 12th-century Danish chronicle through a French intermediary. King Lear draws on a 12th-century Welsh chronicle and an earlier play. Romeo and Juliet comes from an Italian novella through an English poem.

What he added: language, character, philosophical weight. Plutarch gives a few facts about Cleopatra. Shakespeare gives 'Age cannot wither her, nor custom stale / Her infinite variety.' The plot's the same; everything else is his.

This was standard Renaissance practice. Originality of plot was not valued. Originality of treatment was the artistic measure.

concepts.title: The Texts We Have
concepts.contentHtml:
Shakespeare didn't oversee the publication of his plays as literary works. He wrote them as performance scripts.

Some plays appeared during his lifetime in cheap quarto editions, often unauthorized. Some quartos are 'good' (likely from Shakespeare's manuscripts); some are 'bad' (apparently reconstructed from memory by actors).

The First Folio (1623), put together by his theatrical colleagues seven years after his death, is the first systematic collection. It includes 36 plays and is the only source for some of them, including Macbeth, The Tempest, and As You Like It.

What this means: the text you read is the result of editorial decisions about variant readings, missing punctuation, scribal errors. Major plays exist in importantly different versions. The 'King Lear' you read is probably a conflation of two different texts. There is no single authoritative Shakespeare. Editors negotiate.

title: Comedies
description: Twelfth Night, Much Ado, As You Like It — disguise and reconciliation

concepts.title: What Shakespearean Comedy Does
concepts.contentHtml:
Shakespeare's comedies follow a recognizable shape. A young woman or two falls in love. An obstacle intervenes — a parent, a misunderstanding, an unequal social rank. The lovers escape into a wild or pastoral place — a forest, an island, the night. Disguise produces confusion. Eventually the obstacle is overcome. The play ends with marriages, often multiple, and a return to the social order.

The pattern goes back through New Comedy to its Greek and Roman ancestors. Shakespeare's contribution isn't the structure; it's what he does inside it. His comic worlds combine genuine feeling with real wit. They take love seriously without being solemn.

The major mature comedies — A Midsummer Night's Dream (1595), Much Ado About Nothing (1599), As You Like It (1599), Twelfth Night (1602) — were written in a remarkable run within about seven years.

concepts.title: Twelfth Night
concepts.contentHtml:
Twelfth Night (c. 1602) is the central romantic comedy. Twin siblings Viola and Sebastian are separated in a shipwreck. Each thinks the other dead. Viola disguises herself as a young man, Cesario, and enters the service of Duke Orsino. He sends Cesario to court Olivia on his behalf. Olivia falls for Cesario. Viola loves Orsino.

The comic structure works through misdirection. Viola can't reveal her sex without ending Olivia's affection but also her own employment. Olivia's affections only resolve when Sebastian appears and is mistaken for Cesario.

Beneath the comedy: melancholy. Viola's love for Orsino is constrained, unspoken; her brother is presumed dead. Malvolio, the puritanical steward, is cruelly humiliated in a subplot whose treatment troubles modern audiences. The play ends with marriages but also with the stranded Antonio, the displaced Malvolio, the unsettled Feste singing 'the rain it raineth every day.'

The comedies aren't all jokes. Their happiness is earned and partial.

concepts.title: Much Ado About Nothing
concepts.contentHtml:
Much Ado About Nothing (c. 1598) pairs a romantic plot with a battle-of-wits plot. Hero and Claudio love each other; Beatrice and Benedick despise each other and trade insults.

The romantic plot turns dark. Claudio is tricked into believing Hero has been unfaithful. He humiliates her at the altar. She faints, is presumed dead, recovers, eventually forgives him.

The witty plot is the heart of the play. Beatrice and Benedick are tricked into believing each other secretly in love, and the ruse becomes truth. Their banter, their resistance to the conventional courtship plot, their genuine intelligence — all make them the most adult lovers in Shakespeare.

Beatrice's 'Kill Claudio' moment, when she demands Benedick avenge Hero's humiliation, is one of the most arresting in the comedies. It tests whether his love is talk or action.

concepts.title: As You Like It and the Pastoral
concepts.contentHtml:
As You Like It (c. 1599) takes the comic form into the forest.

Rosalind, banished from court, flees to the Forest of Arden disguised as a young man, Ganymede. There she encounters her beloved Orlando, also banished. Disguised, she counsels him on courtship — including how to court her, the real Rosalind.

The play's pleasure is its theatrical doubleness. Rosalind is a woman played (originally) by a boy disguised as a man pretending to be a woman. The layers compound. The play's central scenes are extended courtship games where 'Ganymede' and Orlando enact wooing as performance.

The forest is a pastoral space — outside court politics, outside fixed social roles. People sing. Shepherds and shepherdesses appear. Two characters meet, marry, return to court. The forest's job is to allow transformations the court won't permit.

Rosalind herself is one of the great comic roles. She has more lines than any female character in Shakespeare. Her wit, kindness, and theatrical inventiveness make her, for many, his most appealing creation.

concepts.title: The Problem Comedies
concepts.contentHtml:
Some plays Shakespeare wrote between 1600 and 1605 sit awkwardly on the comic side. All's Well That Ends Well, Measure for Measure, Troilus and Cressida. They have the structure of comedies — eventual marriages and reconciliations — but the moral atmosphere is uncomfortable.

In Measure for Measure, a young woman is asked to sleep with a corrupt official to save her brother's life. The play resolves the situation through trickery, but the trickery itself is troubling. The duke who restores order has been spying and manipulating throughout. The comic ending asks more than it answers.

These plays have been called 'dark comedies' or 'problem comedies.' They mark a transition: Shakespeare in the same years began writing his great tragedies. The romantic-comedy form had reached, for him, some kind of limit.

The romantic comedies remained a major influence. Their pattern of disguise, mistaken identity, witty banter, and forest escape recurs across English-language comedy from Restoration to Hollywood.

title: Histories
description: Richard II, Henry IV-V — kingship, time, the nation

concepts.title: What the History Plays Are
concepts.contentHtml:
Shakespeare's history plays dramatize episodes from English royal history, mostly from the late 14th to the late 15th century. Eight of them form two tetralogies.

The first tetralogy (written first, in the early 1590s, but covering the later events): Henry VI Parts 1-3, Richard III.

The second tetralogy (written later, but covering earlier events): Richard II, Henry IV Parts 1-2, Henry V.

Plus standalones: King John, Henry VIII.

The plays were not just historical drama. They were political theater, written when memory of the Wars of the Roses (1455-1487) was still alive and the question of legitimate succession was openly fraught — Elizabeth I had no children, so who would succeed her was a live question.

concepts.title: Richard II
concepts.contentHtml:
Richard II (c. 1595) is the most poetically accomplished of the histories. Its protagonist is a king deposed by his cousin Bolingbroke, who becomes Henry IV.

The play's central question: what is a king? Richard speaks lyrically, indulgently, abstractly about kingship. He believes in his divine right. Bolingbroke speaks practically, decisively, in plainer language. He acts.

Richard's political incompetence — confiscating Bolingbroke's inheritance, raising taxes, surrounding himself with favorites — undoes him. But his fall is treated as poetic, even tragic. The deposition scene (Act 4, Scene 1) is one of the great set pieces in Shakespeare. Richard hands over his crown speaking in elaborate metaphor about identity and loss.

The play sets up a question for the rest of the second tetralogy: was Bolingbroke's deposition of an anointed king justified? It's a political question with serious theological dimensions in Shakespeare's England.

concepts.title: Henry IV and Falstaff
concepts.contentHtml:
The two parts of Henry IV (c. 1597-98) follow the troubled reign of Bolingbroke as Henry IV and the wayward maturation of his son Prince Hal (the future Henry V).

Hal spends his time in Eastcheap taverns with Sir John Falstaff — old, fat, witty, cowardly, dishonest, irresistibly alive. The Hal-Falstaff plot runs alongside scenes of court and battlefield, alternating high politics with low comedy.

Falstaff is, by general consent, Shakespeare's greatest comic creation. Harold Bloom called him one of the few characters in literature to seem more real than the people we actually know. He's a coward who delivers brilliant speeches on cowardice. A liar whose lies are works of art. A drunk who is, in some inverted sense, the moral center of the plays.

By the end of 2 Henry IV, Hal becomes king and rejects Falstaff in public ('I know thee not, old man'). The rejection is one of the most painful scenes in Shakespeare. Becoming king, Hal becomes diminished as a person. Power costs Falstaff. It also costs Hal.

concepts.title: Henry V
concepts.contentHtml:
Henry V (c. 1599) closes the second tetralogy with the new king's victory at Agincourt against the French.

Read straight, it's a triumphant patriotic drama. Henry rallies his outnumbered men with the great 'St. Crispin's Day' speech ('We few, we happy few, we band of brothers'). Against impossible odds, the English win.

Read against the grain — and Shakespeare gives us the resources for either reading — Henry is a calculating politician. He has the French prisoners executed. He claims his cause is just but presses his counselors to confirm a legal case he wants. He is a great king, partly because he has set aside the human openness Hal had.

The play has been used to recruit soldiers in two World Wars. It has also been read as critique. The text supports both. This double-reading is a Shakespearean signature.

concepts.title: Richard III
concepts.contentHtml:
Beyond the second tetralogy: Richard III (c. 1592-93), Shakespeare's first masterpiece.

Richard, Duke of Gloucester, is deformed and embittered. He vows to be a villain. He systematically murders his way to the throne — including his brother, two royal nephews, his wife. The play is essentially a chronicle of his rise and (very brief) fall.

What makes it work is Richard's voice. He addresses the audience directly, explaining his schemes, sharing his contempt for those he deceives. We become his accomplices. He is repulsive and irresistible at once.

The play has been criticized as Tudor propaganda — Richard III's dynasty had been replaced by Elizabeth's grandfather, so blackening Richard served the regime. Modern historians find the historical Richard much less monstrous than Shakespeare paints him. But the dramatic Richard is something else: a study in how charisma and evil can coexist.

Olivier's 1955 film fixed Richard for generations. Subsequent productions have continued to find new ways into him. The role remains one of the great showcase parts in English drama.

title: Tragedies
description: Hamlet, Lear, Macbeth, Othello — the unfathomable plays

concepts.title: The Great Run
concepts.contentHtml:
Between roughly 1599 and 1606, Shakespeare wrote his major tragedies: Hamlet, Othello, King Lear, Macbeth, Antony and Cleopatra, Coriolanus. Plus Julius Caesar and Timon of Athens. About one tragedy per year.

Why? Why this concentration? No one knows. Personal events — his son Hamnet had died in 1596, his father in 1601 — may have mattered. The accession of James I in 1603 created a darker political mood. The form itself, after the comedies and histories, may have demanded he take it on.

What's certain: this is the most concentrated production of major tragedies in any literature. Together they redefine what a tragedy can do.

concepts.title: Hamlet
concepts.contentHtml:
Hamlet (c. 1600) is the most discussed play ever written. The plot: Prince Hamlet's father is murdered by his uncle Claudius, who marries Hamlet's mother and takes the throne. The ghost of the father charges Hamlet with revenge. Hamlet delays.

The delay is the play. Hamlet philosophizes, performs madness, harangues his mother, drives Ophelia mad and to suicide, kills the wrong man, plots a play within the play to test his uncle. He doesn't act until the final scene, when everyone dies.

Why does he delay? Cowardice? Doubt about the ghost? Oedipal entanglement? Existential paralysis? The play supports each reading. Hamlet himself doesn't know. His soliloquies — 'To be, or not to be,' 'How all occasions do inform against me' — are explorations of his own incapacity.

What makes Hamlet inexhaustible is that he seems to think more than the play can show. He outruns his own circumstances. Every generation has projected its philosophy onto him: Romantic introspective, Freudian son, existentialist hero, postmodern questioner. The play is roomy enough for all.

concepts.title: King Lear
concepts.contentHtml:
King Lear (c. 1605) is the bleakest and many think the deepest of the tragedies.

An aging king divides his kingdom among his three daughters based on which one declares the most love for him. The youngest, Cordelia, refuses to flatter and is disinherited. Her two flattering sisters, having received the kingdom, abuse and betray Lear. Lear goes mad on a heath in a storm. A subplot follows the parallel betrayal of the Earl of Gloucester by his bastard son Edmund.

The play's vision is unforgiving. Cordelia, who has done nothing wrong, is hanged. Lear dies cradling her body. The good characters die almost as readily as the bad. There is no theological consolation.

What survives is human bond. Lear in the storm, having lost everything, recognizes for the first time the suffering of the poor. Edgar guides his blind father. Kent serves Lear in disguise. The play does not promise that these bonds save anyone. They are what's there.

Tolstoy hated King Lear. Most subsequent readers have come to see it as Shakespeare's most ambitious play.

concepts.title: Macbeth
concepts.contentHtml:
Macbeth (c. 1606) is the shortest of the major tragedies and the tightest. It's also the only tragedy whose protagonist commits the central crime.

Macbeth, a Scottish general, encounters three witches who prophesy he will be king. His wife pushes him to murder the king to fulfill the prophecy. He does. He then kills more people to maintain his position. He goes mad with guilt and paranoia. He is killed.

What's distinctive: we follow Macbeth from before the crime to after, with full access to his consciousness. We watch a person become a murderer. The transformation is gradual, partial, never complete. He never stops being capable of moral perception — he just stops acting on it.

Lady Macbeth is one of Shakespeare's most extraordinary creations. She drives the murder, then breaks under it. Her sleepwalking scene ('Out, damned spot!') gives us the consequences his more rationalizing soliloquies don't.

The play is dense with moral weight per line. It's the play to start with for someone new to Shakespeare's tragedies — short, focused, devastating.

concepts.title: Othello
concepts.contentHtml:
Othello (c. 1604) is the most painful of the tragedies because the destruction is so unnecessary.

Othello, a Moor and a great general, has secretly married Desdemona, a Venetian noblewoman who loves him. His ensign Iago, for reasons he gives variously and never quite explains, decides to destroy them. He plants false suspicion that Desdemona is unfaithful. Othello believes him. He smothers Desdemona in their bed. Then, learning the truth, he kills himself.

The play's horror is its progression from intimacy to murder, watched in close detail. Othello's transformation, scene by scene, from confident lover to jealous monster, is one of the most disturbing things in Shakespeare. It happens entirely through Iago's manipulation of words and circumstantial evidence.

The play has been read in many ways: as a study of jealousy, as a meditation on race and outsider status in early modern Europe, as a tragedy about self-deception. Iago — perhaps Shakespeare's most evil character — has fascinated audiences and frightened them. His final line, refusing to explain himself: 'Demand me nothing. What you know, you know.'

title: Romances & Late Plays
description: The Tempest, Winter's Tale — magic and forgiveness

concepts.title: The Late Style
concepts.contentHtml:
Around 1607-1611, Shakespeare's mode changed. The tragedies stopped. He wrote four plays — Pericles, Cymbeline, The Winter's Tale, The Tempest — that have come to be called the romances or late plays.

They are tragicomedies. Disasters happen — children lost, wives accused, kingdoms torn apart — but the disasters are reversed. Lost children return. Apparently dead wives are restored. The plays end with reconciliation rather than catastrophe.

The mood is strange. Time spans are long — sometimes 16 years between halves. Magic and supernatural events recur. Music plays a larger role. The verse becomes more compressed, less smooth, more allusive — what scholars call Shakespeare's late style.

concepts.title: The Winter's Tale
concepts.contentHtml:
The Winter's Tale (c. 1611) starts as a tragedy and ends as a romance.

Leontes, king of Sicilia, becomes irrationally jealous of his pregnant wife Hermione, accusing her of an affair with his best friend. He throws her in prison. The newborn daughter is exposed in the wilderness. Hermione apparently dies. The court denounces Leontes' madness. Sixteen years pass.

Then the second half. The exposed daughter Perdita has been raised by shepherds in Bohemia. She falls in love with the prince. The play moves to pastoral comedy. Eventually all return to Sicilia. Perdita is recognized. And — in one of the most extraordinary scenes in Shakespeare — Hermione, presumed dead, appears as a statue that comes to life.

What does the play mean? Time heals. Repentance might restore. Loss is partial. Even within a play that begins with destructive jealousy, recovery is possible — if you're willing to wait sixteen years and accept what's lost.

The shepherd scene in Act 4 is one of the longest comic interludes in Shakespeare and one of the most charming. The 'statue' scene at the end is one of the strangest.

concepts.title: The Tempest
concepts.contentHtml:
The Tempest (c. 1611) is probably Shakespeare's last play written alone. It has often been read as his farewell to the stage.

Prospero, a deposed duke, has been on a remote island for twelve years with his daughter Miranda and the spirit Ariel. He uses his magical powers to wreck a ship containing his enemies and bring them under his power. Over a single day on the island, he tests them, his daughter falls in love with one of them, and he forgives them all. He renounces his magic and prepares to return to Milan.

The play has been read endlessly: as colonial allegory (Caliban, the island's original inhabitant, enslaved by Prospero), as theatrical autobiography (Prospero's renunciation as Shakespeare's), as meditation on art and forgiveness.

Prospero's epilogue, asking the audience for applause to release him from the stage, is one of the most moving moments in Shakespeare. Whether or not Shakespeare consciously intended it as goodbye, it functions as one.

concepts.title: What the Late Plays Do
concepts.contentHtml:
Why does Shakespeare turn from tragedy to these strange tragicomedies?

Possible reasons. Audience taste was shifting; the Blackfriars indoor theater (which Shakespeare's company started using around 1608) suited spectacle and music more than the open Globe had. The death of his son Hamnet 15 years earlier may have surfaced now in plots about lost-then-found children. Personal mood may have softened.

What the late plays add to Shakespeare's range: a willingness to allow restoration. The tragedies refuse easy comfort; the comedies require none. The late plays imagine restoration that isn't easy — that takes time, suffering, and waiting.

This pattern has been hugely influential. Critics have since traced a 'late style' in artists from Beethoven to Henry James; Edward Said's book On Late Style made the idea central. The idea of an artist turning, near the end, toward forgiveness rather than indictment owes a lot to Shakespeare.

concepts.title: Collaboration and Final Years
concepts.contentHtml:
Modern scholarship has confirmed that Shakespeare collaborated more than once thought. Pericles is partly by George Wilkins. The Two Noble Kinsmen and Henry VIII are partly by John Fletcher, Shakespeare's successor as the King's Men's leading playwright. Some early plays may have parts by other hands too.

This wasn't unusual. Theatrical writing in early modern England was often collaborative. What's unusual is that Shakespeare did so much alone. Most of his contemporaries wrote in teams more often.

Around 1613, Shakespeare retired to Stratford-upon-Avon, where he had been buying property for years. He died there on April 23, 1616, on what may have been his 52nd birthday.

His last writings include the late romances and the collaborative plays. He left no final testament about his work. The First Folio, seven years later, is what preserved him for us. Without it, his career would look very different.

title: Sonnets & Verse
description: The 154 sonnets, the dark lady, the fair youth

concepts.title: The Sonnets
concepts.contentHtml:
Shakespeare's 154 sonnets were published in 1609, probably without his authorization. They form one of the great poetic sequences in English.

Each is 14 lines of iambic pentameter, in the English (or Shakespearean) form: three quatrains rhymed ABAB CDCD EFEF, ending with a couplet GG. The form's structural pressure — building an argument across the quatrains, resolving or twisting in the couplet — gives the sonnets their characteristic weight.

Shakespeare didn't invent the form (Surrey did); he made it inexhaustible. After Shakespeare, the English sonnet became one of the most-attempted and least-successfully-achieved forms in the language.

concepts.title: The Fair Youth
concepts.contentHtml:
The first 126 sonnets are addressed to a young man — beautiful, aristocratic, somewhat unreliable — known as the Fair Youth.

The early sonnets (1-17) urge him to marry and have children to perpetuate his beauty. Then the sequence pivots: the speaker himself loves the young man, and the question becomes how to preserve the beloved through poetry rather than through reproduction.

The sonnets to the young man are some of the most intense male-male love poetry in any literature. Sonnet 18 ('Shall I compare thee to a summer's day?'), Sonnet 29 ('When in disgrace with fortune and men's eyes'), Sonnet 116 ('Let me not to the marriage of true minds'). Whether the love was sexual or platonic is debated and probably unanswerable.

Some sonnets are bitter — accusing the young man of betrayal, of sleeping with the speaker's mistress, of preferring a rival poet. The relationship is not idealized.

concepts.title: The Dark Lady
concepts.contentHtml:
Sonnets 127-152 are addressed to a woman, the Dark Lady. She has dark eyes, dark hair, dark complexion — pointedly the opposite of the conventional sonnet heroine of the period (golden hair, light eyes, alabaster skin).

The mood is darker too. The speaker loves and resents her. He knows she is unfaithful. He goes back anyway. Sonnet 130 — 'My mistress' eyes are nothing like the sun' — parodies the conventional praise the Dark Lady doesn't receive. Sonnet 138 — 'When my love swears that she is made of truth, / I do believe her, though I know she lies.'

The sequence ends with mythological sonnets about Cupid, suggesting the speaker has worked himself into resignation about love rather than out of it.

Who was the Dark Lady? Theories: a court musician named Emilia Lanier, the courtesan Lucy Negro, others. As with the Fair Youth, the historical identification doesn't really matter for reading the poems.

concepts.title: What the Sonnets Do
concepts.contentHtml:
Many great sonnets have been written. Shakespeare's are exceptional in particular ways.

Compression. A Shakespearean sonnet has 140 syllables. He gets a complete argument plus a turn into that space, repeatedly.

Voice. The 'I' of the sonnets feels less like a literary persona than other sonneteers'. The speaker contradicts himself, attacks himself, knows he's deceiving himself. Petrarchan posing falls away.

Time. The sonnets are obsessed with time and decay. 'Time' is among the most-used words. The poems try to outlast death by capturing love in language. Many succeed: 'So long lives this, and this gives life to thee.'

Variability. The 154 poems include praise, blame, philosophy, complaint, jokes, devastation. The sequence resists single interpretation.

If you have to start somewhere with the sonnets: 18, 29, 30, 55, 73, 94, 116, 129, 130, 138, 144. Eleven sonnets that show the range.

concepts.title: The Other Verse and Influence
concepts.contentHtml:
Beyond the sonnets, Shakespeare wrote two long narrative poems early in his career: Venus and Adonis (1593) and The Rape of Lucrece (1594). Both are Ovidian — drawing on classical mythology, polished, occasionally lavish. They were popular bestsellers in his lifetime.

Within the plays, the verse achievements are extraordinary. Most of Shakespeare's plays are written in blank verse — unrhymed iambic pentameter, the meter that came to dominate English drama. Marlowe had popularized it before Shakespeare; Shakespeare made it flexible enough to hold any kind of speech.

His influence on subsequent English verse is immeasurable. Milton built on his blank verse. Wordsworth claimed inheritance. Keats studied him obsessively. Eliot wrote the central modern essay on him. Hughes, Bishop, Heaney, Walcott — countless 20th-century poets define their work in relation to him.

One way to take Shakespeare's full measure: try to write a passable iambic pentameter line. It's harder than it looks. Then try a Shakespearean speech. The combination of metrical control, syntactic flexibility, and emotional weight per line is what makes him irreproducible.
